entries.title: Justice Department can no longer pressure Facebook, Apple to remove ICE-sighting apps, judge rules
entries.summary: <p>A federal judge has ordered the Justice Department and U.S. Department of Homeland Security not to pressure Facebook and Apple from banning ICE-monitoring apps and social media groups.</p><p>The preliminary injunction ruling, issued last week by U.S. District Judge Jorge Alonso, stems from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/12/chicago-area-resident-lawsuit-facebook-ice-tracking-app" target="_blank" >a lawsuit filed in February by Kassandra “Kae” Rosado</a> against former U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi and U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem.</p><p>Rosado alleges that both federal agencies coerced Facebook into removing her “ICE Sighting-Chicagoland” group, which aimed to keep residents informed about where U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents were seen in the Chicago area.</p><p>Mark Hodges, an Indiana resident who created the mobile app Eyes Up, which allowed users to record, securely store and view videos of ICE officers committing potential civil rights violations, also joined the lawsuit. The lawsuit claims Apple removed Hodges’ app from the App Store in October — during the height of the Trump administration’s “Operation Midway Blitz” deportation campaign — after pressure from the federal government.</p><p>The judge’s order says Justice Department and DHS officials can no longer take actions to demand or pressure Facebook to suppress Rosado’s Facebook group or pressure Apple to suppress Hodges’ app.</p><p>The Justice Department and DHS were given until Tuesday to notify its employees, Facebook’s parent company Meta, and Apple of the order, and to file a status report documenting the agencies’ actions to comply.</p><p>Rosado’s group had nearly 100,000 members in October and had thousands of posts and comments per day about immigration-related arrests and violent interactions with immigration agents across the Chicago area.</p><p>On Oct. 12, right-wing activist and Trump ally Laura Loomer <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/LauraLoomer/status/1977345952718438707" target="_blank" >tagged</a> the Justice Department and DHS leaders in a post claiming that the Facebook page and others like it “are getting people killed.” The next day, Loomer said in a post that a Justice Department source told her that they had contacted executives at Meta, “to tell them they need to remove these ICE tracking pages from the platform.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/a8/31/3c4137a74795885492c17aa7137c/show-temp-14.pdf" target="_blank" ><i>Read the preliminary injunction</i></a><i>:</i></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://docs.google.com/viewer?embedded=true&url=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/a8/31/3c4137a74795885492c17aa7137c/show-temp-14.pdf"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: Man’s bid for a retrial in boy’s murder hinges on ex-Chicago cop’s alleged ties to Gitmo torture
entries.summary: <p>A man who says Chicago police beat him into confessing to the 1992 murder of 7-year-old Dantrell Davis is a step closer to finding out whether he’ll get a new trial.</p><p>One of Anthony Garrett’s attorneys battled a Cook County prosecutor in closing arguments Monday afternoon at the Leighton Criminal Courthouse.</p><p>The attorney, Jennifer Blagg, argued that retired Detective Richard Zuley, 79, coordinated her client's torture. She tied the case to alleged <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/04/13/settlement-finance-committee-richard-zuley-chicago-detective-carl-reed-coerced-confession" target="_blank" >Zuley-led coercion</a> in a string of cases from 1987 to 2003, including four murder convictions that were later thrown out.</p><p>“He’s never in the room when the worst stuff happens, but he doesn’t have to be [because the officers] are all working together,” Blagg said.</p><p>She also likened Garrett’s case to torture that happened when Zuley was a U.S. Naval reservist at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba. She recounted November testimony by Mohamedou Ould Slahi, 55, who appeared via Zoom from Rotterdam, the Dutch city.</p><p>Slahi, a Sept. 11 terror suspect, alleged that Zuley subjected him to months of torture in 2003 at the notorious detention camp at Guantánamo.</p><p>Slahi wrote a memoir about the experience that formed the basis of a 2021 film drama starring Jodie Foster and Benedict Cumberbatch.</p><p>“The real Dick Zuley, I would submit to the court, is the one Mohamedou Ould Slahi saw,” Blagg said Monday.</p><p>But the prosecutor, Armando G. Sandoval, urged Judge Adrienne E. Davis to disregard claims against Zuley in other cases, calling them “allegations, not findings,” and saying they “have no connection to Garrett.”</p><p>“I’m not saying everything Slahi says is false,” Sandoval said. “But the court should be careful of treating the book … or the movie as objective.”</p><p>Sandoval also cast doubt on claims by Garrett that two large men wearing sports jerseys beat him at Zuley’s behest while he was shackled to an eyebolt, and that the two men focused many of their blows on a part of his leg where physicians had implanted a rod after a gunshot wound.</p><p>The prosecutor pointed to testimony that Garrett, after his interrogation, was not limping and did not seem to be injured.</p><p>Sandoval also noted Garrett’s initial claim that the beating took place with a rubber hose. The story changed years later, Sandoval said, when Garrett claimed it was carried out with the hose and a phone book.</p><p>“His account shifts,” Sandoval said. “That’s important.”</p><p>Dantrell was killed on Oct. 13, 1992, as he walked to school with his mother from Cabrini-Green, a former North Side public housing complex. Police said a sniper shot him from an upper floor of a building.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" </div> </div><p>A jury convicted Garrett in 1994. Now 67, he’s imprisoned at downstate Centralia Correctional Center. He’s not scheduled for release until 2039, according to the Illinois Department of Corrections.</p><p>Monday’s proceedings stem from a 2023 referral by the Illinois Torture and Relief Commission that detailed an “overwhelming” history of “lengthy and consistent” complaints alleging psychological and physical torture involving Zuley. He was hired by CPD in 1970 and worked more than three decades for the department.</p><p>Slahi, who knew Zuley as Capt. Collins, testified the detective led <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2025/11/25/mohamedou-ould-slahi-guantanamo-chicago-police-richard-zuley-anthony-garrett-torture-dantrell-davis" target="_blank" >“enhanced interrogation techniques,”</a> including isolation, temperature extremes, beatings, sexual humiliation, sleep deprivation, waterboarding, barking dogs, a mock execution at sea, and round-the-clock mistreatment with strobe lights and a looped recording of the U.S. national anthem.</p><p>After 70 days of torture, Slahi testified, the detective convinced him that U.S. authorities were allowing his mother to be kidnapped and raped. Slahi admitted he never saw Zuley lay a hand on him but added that he wouldn’t know because he was usually blindfolded.</p><p>Slahi testified he eventually confessed to anything his interrogators fed him, starting with plans to attack Toronto’s CN Tower. He said he also falsely confirmed that many individuals had Al Qaeda links.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/04/08/ex-gitmo-detainee-could-air-allegations-of-torture-by-former-chicago-detective" target="_blank" >Slahi was held at Guantánamo</a> for 14 years without charges before he was released to his native Mauritania in 2016. His memoirs about those years were published as a book that led to the film, “The Mauritanian,” directed by Kevin Macdonald.</p><p>At a November hearing, a prosecutor pressed Slahi about visits to Afghanistan in the early 1990s. Slahi answered he was working for U.S. allies there and cut Al Qaeda ties years before the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/02/19/ex-chicago-det-richard-zuley-denies-torturing-out-confession-to-7-year-old-dantrell-daviss-murder" target="_blank" >Zuley testified</a> at Feb. 18 and April 1 hearings in Garrett’s case. The former detective said he didn’t know of anyone at the police station handcuffing Garrett to the eyebolt or subjecting him to any physical or mental abuse.</p><p>Zuley testified he left other detectives in charge of Garrett overnight. The next morning, the former detective said, Garrett said he had fired at members of a rival gang near Dantrell. Garrett later signed a handwritten confession.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a70000" name="image-a70000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5aee1be/2147483647/strip/true/crop/632x355+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbc%2Ffd%2Fec8693cb405a8749cacc3501ea56%2Fscreenshot-2025-04-07-at-10-18-19-pm.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d4ba8a4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/632x355+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbc%2Ffd%2Fec8693cb405a8749cacc3501ea56%2Fscreenshot-2025-04-07-at-10-18-19-pm.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1c2a5e8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/632x355+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbc%2Ffd%2Fec8693cb405a8749cacc3501ea56%2Fscreenshot-2025-04-07-at-10-18-19-pm.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Anthony Garrett is imprisoned at Centralia Correctional Center. entries.title: Sky face first true playoff-caliber test against Valkyries
entries.summary: <p>SAN FRANCISCO — Beating the Fire in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/05/09/sky-survive-first-road-test-against-fire" >the regular-season opener </a>was a good sign for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a>.</p><p>Sure, the Fire are an expansion franchise that won't sniff the playoffs this season. But you don't scoff at any wins if you're the Sky. Not when you scraped together only 10 of them last year. Not when four of your top eight players were watching in street clothes.</p><p>You can earn a few stripes beating a bad team short-handed.</p><p>But you really earn your "good-team" credentials by beating other good teams.</p><p>The Sky get their shot Wednesday night against the Valkyries. Another sellout crowd, another hostile environment. The first real chance to prove they belong in the playoff conversation.</p><p>Plenty to worry about until then.</p><p>The second half against the Fire flashed a few warning signs. Shooters left wide open in transition. Point guards dribbling the length of the floor without anyone stepping up to stop them.</p><p>At practice Monday, coach Tyler Marsh called it "coverage slippage" that needed to be cleaned up.</p><p>It will need to be squeaky clean against the Valkyries.</p><p>Golden State is well-coached, on a mission, and dangerous at every position. Their backup center, Janelle Salaun, makes it rain from deep in ways most Sky starters don't. Guards Veronica Burton and Gabby Williams make a living getting into the paint.</p><p>"A lot of their offense is based on engaging two," Natasha Cloud told the Sun-Times. "Coming off ball screens, engaging two defenders and they're really great at [making the extra pass]. As much as we can, we've got to guard our yard and take pride in our individual defense so that we're not coming into our secondary and third level of help."</p><p>Having a versatile defender like Cloud back will certainly help. But the Valkyries’ offense challenges the exact two weak points of the Sky's defense last season: containing dribble penetration and defending the arc. Time to show that this year is different.</p><p>Sky players and coaches keep pointing to the athleticism, quickness, and length on the new roster as reasons to believe they can be better defensively. Those are solid ingredients, but they won’t come together without a recipe. Does Marsh have one?</p><p>Wednesday will give us a clue.</p><p>For now, there's enough from the Fire game for Marsh to feel good about.</p><p>The offense looked cohesive. The Skylar Diggins-Kamilla Cardoso pick-and-roll was cooking.</p><p>And when the Sky looked like they were about to throw away a lead — like they did so often last season — they said, no, actually, we're not doing that. Not this time.</p><p>This year, they have Diggins' leadership to fall back on. Someone to step up and hit a big fourth-quarter three — not even her specialty — then throw her head back, stick her tongue out, let the crowd know the party is over.</p><p>The Sky also got a clutch performance from veteran center Elizabeth Williams, who came off the bench to deliver blocks and buckets when it mattered most.</p><p>Those are foundational elements to build on.</p><p>"We got to come with the same level of focus and be able to clean up the areas that we need to, but also stay true to the things that we did well coming out of Portland," Marsh said.</p><p>Clean it up and stay true. entries.title: RJ Day, son of Ohio State coach Ryan Day, commits to Northwestern
entries.summary: <p>Quarterback RJ Day said he is committing to play at Northwestern beginning in 2027, putting him in line to join his father in the Big Ten Conference.</p><p>The son of Ohio State football coach Ryan Day announced his decision this weekend on social media.</p><p>"Excited for the next step and ready to get to work," Day posted in a message thanking coaches and family.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Super excited to announce my commitment to further my football and academic career at Northwestern University!! Thank you to everyone along my journey who has made this possible from my family, <a href="https://twitter.com/BradMaendler?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@BradMaendler</a> , the Desales coaching staff and Jay Hooten at the Armory. Excited for… <a href="https://t.co/3hLTnjsdSf">pic.twitter.com/3hLTnjsdSf</a></p>— RJ Day (@rj_day1) <a href="https://twitter.com/rj_day1/status/2053476361520468049?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">May 10, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Chip Kelly is the offensive coordinator on coach David Braun's staff at Northwestern after serving in that role under Day when the Buckeyes won the national championship in the 2024 season. Kelly was also the offensive coordinator when Ryan Day played QB at New Hampshire and set nine school records.</p><p>RJ Day plays at St. Francis DeSales High School in Columbus, Ohio.</p>

entries.title: White Sox have come a long way, baby
entries.summary: <p>At the quarter mark of the 2026 season, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> are easily in the best shape they have been in the standings in four years.</p><p>There was nowhere to go but up after three consecutive seasons with 100 or more losses. You can measure the Sox’ improvement by the numbers, not just the vibe.</p><p>Forty games into the 162-game schedule, the Sox are 19-21. It’s their best 40-game start since 2022, when they were 20-20 on May 21 after taking the first game of a doubleheader against the Yankees.</p><p>That .500 record foreshadowed an 81-81 season that started a rapid disintegration of a team that was supposed to do big things.</p><p>Here’s where the Sox stand after 40 games and where they stood in each of the last three painful seasons:</p><p>• 2026: 19-21, 171 runs scored, 185 runs allowed. Final record: ?</p><p>• 2025: 11-29, 135 runs scored, 172 runs allowed. Final record: 60-102.</p><p>• 2024: 12-28, 119 runs scored, 202 runs allowed. Final record 41-121, setting a modern-era record for losses.</p><p>• 2023: 13-27, 169 runs scored, 241 runs allowed. Final record: 61-101.</p><p>‘‘If you look at it on a daily basis, on a nightly basis, we feel like we have a chance to win,’’ general manager Chris Getz said at the start of the Sox’ homestand. ‘‘In the past, it was more [that] you almost needed to be perfect.</p><p>‘‘Now the lineup is deeper. You know the rotation is deeper. We’ve got some weapons in the bullpen that will allow us to navigate and finish off games. And the defense is improved.’’</p><p>A marquee slugger in Munetaka Murakami has made a difference. Big-presence batters who flirt with the major-league home-run lead not only generate deep drives and headlines, they also change the dynamics of a lineup.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/05/11/cubs-seiya-suzuki-counsels-white-sox-munetaka-murakami-kazuma-okamoto-shohei-ohtani" >Cubs’ Seiya Suzuki counsels White Sox’ Munetaka Murakami about life in Chicago</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Second-year shortstop Colson Montgomery hopes to take advantage of it as he continues to adjust to major-league pitching.</p><p>‘‘It’s completely different,’’ Montgomery said before the Sox’ 2-1, come-from-behind victory Sunday against the Mariners. ‘‘We have guys at the end of our lineup who get on base a lot. We have more guys able to put the ball in the seats and hit home runs. I think it’s all really good.’’</p><p>Beyond Murakami, Montgomery points to third baseman Miguel Vargas, who has been striking the ball with authority more consistently.</p><p>‘‘Yeah, I think me, Mune and Vargas are all really good at [being run-producers],’’ Montgomery said. ‘‘It just feels like every single time I’m up to bat, either Vargas or Mune, they are on base. There’s opportunities to drive guys in.’’</p><p>Despite injuries, such as to catcher Kyle Teel and outfielder Everson Pereira, the Sox’ offense is at its best through 40 games since 2022. They were an AL-leading 25-15 and had scored 216 runs at this point en route to winning the AL Central at 93-69 in 2021.</p><p>Montgomery is hitting only .221, but he has 10 homers and 28 RBI through 40 games. Murakami has 15 homers and 29 RBI with a .232 average and, as expected, 60 strikeouts in 173 plate appearances. Vargas is batting .230 with nine homers and 22 RBI.</p><p>But don’t let the low averages be a guide, Montgomery said.</p><p>‘‘I don’t look at my average; I don’t,’’ Montgomery said. ‘‘I know a lot of people are like, ‘They only hit this amount.’ But I just look at production and on-base percentage, OPS, things like that. Those things are what’s going to help you win games.’’</p><p>The Sox’ .231 batting average is 25th in the majors and 13th in the AL. Their run production, however, isn’t as low: 18th in MLB and ninth in the AL.</p><p>Then there are the intangibles. The Sox have been upbeat, not moping their way to the bottom. ‘‘A young, aggressive team having fun’’ seems to be a common theme.</p><p>‘‘We’re looking for winning-type players that are focused on, you know, ‘What am I going to do to help this team win?’ ’’ Getz said. ‘‘And that’s starting to seep into this organization as a whole.’’</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: Man who helped grad student stabbed downtown tells jury the alleged killer later pulled a knife on him
entries.summary: <p>A man who ran to help visiting graduate student Anat Kimchi after she was fatally stabbed in a random attack downtown in June 2021 testified Monday that he saw defendant Tony Robinson attack her and that Robinson later threatened him with a knife.</p><p>The witness, Tavon Jones, said he was homeless at the time. He told the court that he had previously seen Robinson, who lived in a tent on Lower Wacker Drive, walking around the area.</p><p>Robinson, 45, is charged with first-degree murder in Kimchi's killing.</p><p>The 31-year-old University of Maryland graduate student was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2021/6/26/22551535/tony-robinson-anat-kimchi-charged-fatally-stabbing-maryland-grad-student-in-the-loop" target="_blank" >killed on a sunny Saturday afternoon</a> on June 19, 2021, near Wacker Drive and Van Buren Street, a short distance from Willis Tower.</p><p>Kimchi's murder was one of several shocking cases examined in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/chicago-downtown-attacks-mental-health-system" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Sun-Times investigation</u></a> last year into violent attacks in the downtown area.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-280000" name="image-280000"></a> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Anat Kimchi, a University of Maryland graduate student, was stabbed to death in 2021 near Lower Wacker Drive, where her alleged killer Tony Robinson was living in a tent.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Robinson's jury trial at the George N. Leighton Criminal Courthouse is overseen by Judge John F. Lyke Jr.</p><p>Jones testified Monday that as he saw Robinson stab Kimchi two times in the back of the neck at 401 S. Wacker Drive, he yelled "no" and ran over to try to stop the attack. Jones said Robinson turned to him and said, "You don’t want none of these problems, big bro."</p><p>Jones testified Robinson then ran away toward Lower Wacker. Jones used Kimchi's phone to call 911 and stayed with her until an ambulance and police arrived.</p><p>On June 22, Jones viewed a photo lineup but was unable to identify Robinson. He testified that at the time, he struggled with substance abuse and was "inebriated" when he looked at the photo lineup.</p><p>Jones testified that the next day, he went to confront Robinson at the tent on Lower Wacker where he heard he was living. Jones testified that Robinson came out, but then "his face changed" and he ducked back into the tent and emerged again holding a knife with "a very specific blade." Jones said Robinson said to him, "What are you doing down here, big bro?"</p><p>Jones said he realized Robinson’s photo had been in the photo array he'd seen a day earlier and told police.</p><p>On June 25, he viewed an in-person lineup at Area 3 detective headquarters and identified Robinson as Kimchi's killer.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" Chukman/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Kimchi had come to Chicago from Maryland to visit a friend.</p><p>Assistant State’s Attorney Anna Sedelmaier told the jury that Kimchi "wasn't bothering anyone, she wasn't looking for any trouble. She was just walking, looking for a place to read a book."</p><p>Her mother, Chava Kimchi-Sarfaty, told the jury that her daughter "was fun to be with, she loves dogs — she had a dog. She was a bright Ph. D. student."</p><p>"For us, she was our daughter. She called me every day … I miss her so much," said Kimchi-Sarfaty, who lives in North Potomac, Maryland.</p><p>Kimchi's father, Avraham, and brothers, Itamar and Ofer, also attended the trial Monday.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-6b0000" name="module-6b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h4><b>FAILURE TO TREAT, FAILURE TO PROTECT</b></h4><i>This investigation by the Sun-Times examines how the failures of the mental health system in Chicago have had deadly consequences and looks at possible solutions.</i><br><h5><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/chicago-downtown-attacks-mental-health-system" >Read more stories in the series > </a></h5></div> </div><p>Robinson's tent on Lower Wacker Drive was near where the killing took place.</p><p>Public defenders Robyn Haynes and Ali Ammoura tried to poke holes in Jones's eyewitness testimony, pointing out inconsistencies in his initial description of the offender to police, including that the killer had "sh--y-ass dreads" and was younger and taller than Robinson is.</p><p>Robinson didn't have dreadlocks at the time of his arrest.</p><p>Jones testified that it was a chaotic scene and that he was focused on the victim.</p><p>"I specifically said 'short dreads,' which is referred to in our community as kinky twists," Jones said in explaining the hair discrepancy.</p><p>According to police and court records, Robinson had a history of arrests and bizarre behavior, including telling detectives "he believes people are following him and tracking his location using their cellphones" and that "he sees people looking at their cellphones and has gone up behind them to look over their shoulder to see if they are tracking him."</p><p>Robinson's arrests started in his teens.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" Chukman/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Authorities say that in the days before Kimchi's killing, Robinson struck a woman in the head in the 500 block of South Franklin Street and three days later hit another woman in the head, breaking her nose, and stole her iPhone and cash near Congress Parkway and South Michigan Avenue. That woman, a tourist from St. Louis in town for a Cubs game, had left a hotel to get coffee when she said she heard Robinson say, "Are you following me?" according to police reports.</p><p>On Monday, Robinson, dressed in a light-colored button-down shirt and black pants and wearing a white cap on his head, spent most of the day facing the jury, leaning back in his chair against the wall of the courtroom.</p><p>In a previous interview with the Sun-Times, Kimchi's family mourned the loss of their daughter, a promising student whose research focus was the criminal justice system.</p><p>She had earned two undergraduate degrees and a master's from the University of Maryland in College Park and was posthumously awarded her doctorate degree two weeks after her death.</p><p>Her research focused on which nonviolent offenders were the most likely to abide by conditions of their early release from prison and which were the likeliest to fail.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/04/10/anat-kimchi-downtown-chicago-random-killings-mentally-ill-tony-robinson-lower-wacker-drive-homeless-tikkun-olam-university-maryland-college-park" target="_blank" >A middle child with two brothers</a>, Kimchi was creative as well as analytical, her family says. She liked writing, dancing and making art, and she was an animal lover.</p><p>Her family emigrated from Israel to the United States when she was 8.</p><p>Her high school in Maryland created an award in her honor to recognize outstanding alumni who contribute to society. It’s called the "Anat Kimchi Award for Excellence in <i>Tikkun Olam</i>," which is a Hebrew phrase that means "repairing the world."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Cubs' Seiya Suzuki counsels White Sox' Munetaka Murakami about life in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>ATLANTA — When Japanese slugger Munetaka Murakami signed with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> this past winter, he reached out to Cubs veteran Seiya Suzuki for advice.</p><p>“[It was] nothing really about baseball,’’ Suzuki said through his translator Sunday morning in Texas before the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> flew to Atlanta to open a three-game set against the Braves that starts Tuesday. “More about Chicago, you know — where to live, where to eat.”</p><p>Because Murakami would be playing on the South Side, Suzuki recommended finding a place downtown.</p><p>“Nearby, and good security,” he said.</p><p>And did Murakami take his advice?</p><p>“I don’t know where he is,” Suzuki said. “I haven’t seen him.”</p><p>That changes this weekend, when Suzuki and the Cubs will travel to Rate Field for the first round of the Crosstown Series with the Sox. The teams meet again in August at Wrigley Field.</p><p>Murakami has been a revelation in his first MLB season, hitting 15 home runs in his first 38 games, which put him third in the majors ahead of play Monday, one homer behind the Yankees’ Aaron Judge and the Phillies’ Kyle Schwarber. He announced his arrival by homering in each of his first three games, then in five straight games from April 17 to 22.</p><p>Can Murakami Mania be far behind, especially with the Sox flirting with first place in the American League Central?</p><p>“I think it’s impressive,” Suzuki said, “especially because the environment has changed for him. If he was putting up those numbers in Japan, I wouldn’t be surprised. But since coming over to a different country and stadium, and he’s still doing the same thing, that’s impressive.”</p><p>Despite hitting 246 home runs in eight seasons with the Tokyo Yakult Swallows of Nippon Professional Baseball’s Central League, including a career-high 56 homers in 2022, Murakami attracted limited interest when he announced his intentions to play in the United States. The Sox, facing limited competition, were able to sign him to a two-year, $34 million deal. Contrast that with the five-year, $85 million deal that Suzuki signed with the Cubs before the 2022 season.</p><p>Murakami already has exceeded the 14 homers Suzuki hit in 111 games during that first season in Chicago.</p><p>“My first year, you know, all of my teammates, everybody was really nice to me,” Suzuki said. “It was nice to be around.</p><p>“But I think, with the [different] food and everything, I think it wasn’t until my second year that I felt acclimated.”</p><p>Suzuki missed the first dozen games of this season after hurting his right knee attempting to steal second base while playing for Japan in the World Baseball Classic against Venezuela, the eventual champion. The injury was diagnosed as a minor sprain of the posterior cruciate ligament, which runs down the back of the knee, connecting the thigh bone to the shinbone. It’s far less common than an injury to the anterior cruciate ligament, according to the Cleveland Clinic, accounting for about 20% of knee ligament injuries.</p><p>Suzuki has recovered to hit seven home runs through the Cubs’ first 41 games, which puts him on a pace to hit 28 this season, four fewer than last season’s 32. The most he hit in a single season in Japan was 38 in 2021, the year before he signed with the Cubs.</p><p>Another Japanese slugger, third baseman Kazuma Okamoto, also made his big-league debut this season, so far hitting 10 home runs for the Blue Jays. He and Murakami are both ahead of Suzuki and Dodgers designated hitter and pitcher Shohei Ohtani, who was off to a slow start with just six home runs, well behind the pace that led to his major-league-best 54 and 55 home runs in 2024 and 2025, respectively.</p><p>All four players represented Team Japan in the WBC this spring. Is there a rivalry?</p><p>“There’s no real sense of competition,” Suzuki said. “It’s more like you check in on what they’re doing, and it gives you a little motivation. You know they’re working hard, and you want to work hard.”</p><p>All four players spoke frequently to each other then, although not as much recently.</p><p>“Everybody’s doing well,” Suzuki said. “I think it’s a good thing, especially for younger Japanese players that aspire to come to Major League Baseball. I think watching us, they’ll work harder.”</p><p>At 26, Murakami is the youngest of the four. Okamoto turns 30 at the end of June, Ohtani 32 in July and Suzuki 32 a month later.</p><p>Veteran reporter Katsushi Nagao of Kyodo News said Suzuki isn’t really regarded in Japan as a prototypical home-run hitter — and doesn’t see himself that way, either.</p><p>“In the spring,” Nagao said, “I would ask Seiya about Murakami, and he would say, ‘It might take him time to get used to [MLB], but he’s going to hit home runs. But not me.”</p><p>Statistics compiled by MLB’s Baseball Savant suggest Suzuki doesn’t have the classic slugger’s uppercut. Murakami, on the other hand, has an attack angle of 19%, which ranks third in MLB. Okamoto is at 16%, Ohtani 13% (like Judge) and Suzuki 10%.</p><p>“In Japan, they’re comparing Shohei and Murakami because Murakami is at such a hot pace,” Nagao said.</p><p>Nagao noted that in Japan, it’s customary to be deferential to your elders.</p><p>“Seiya said to me, ‘I don’t really check [Murakami’s] stats every day, but he’s a nice follower of me.’ They are close, but not like brothers. I’m sure this weekend, they will be chatting with each other.”</p><p>There is a special pride, Suzuki said, in seeing his countrymen thrive.</p><p>“For me, especially when I came over, there were a lot of [Japanese] right-handed hitters who had difficulty adjusting to the league,” he said. “I feel like I was able to kind of break that wall down, where there are plenty of right-handed hitters from Japan who can come over and produce, like Okamoto.</p><p>“I think in Japan right now, the popularity of baseball is going down a little bit — not as many younger kids watching the games. The guys who are playing here now, myself included, want to increase that interest, not only for the fans but for the players who might want to come over.”</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" entries.title: Life and death near Chicago suburbs' booming warehouse hub
entries.summary: <p>It’s a typical weekday afternoon at the intersection of Route 53 and Laraway Road, 40 miles southwest of Chicago, and semi-trucks thunder by in a steady stream.</p><p>They start at the sprawling warehouse complexes on the fringes of Joliet, rumble alongside the fading polyester petals of a roadside memorial for someone who died in a truck crash and roll past the ballfields where youth teams play, carrying goods for Amazon, IKEA, Walmart, Target and Dollar Tree.</p><p>In the next 10 minutes, 150 trucks will pass through the intersection. If you lined them up end to end, they would stretch more than two miles.</p><p>Three decades ago, this area was mostly prairie sprinkled with quiet subdivisions. But the early 2000s ushered in the age of online shopping. Then came the rise of next-day delivery. America’s retailers needed warehouses, fast, and the area outside Chicago — flush with interstates and rail lines — was perfect.</p><p>Few places in the nation have been transformed so completely so quickly. Since 2000, retail giants and developers have erected more than 146 million square feet of warehouse space in the Chicago area — equivalent in size to roughly 1,400 Home Depot stores.</p><p>The warehouses have brought new jobs. Still, people who live nearby say what has happened around them is a cautionary tale for other communities hoping to cash in on the warehouse boom.</p><p>On average, roughly 20,000 trucks pass through Joliet, pop. roughly 150,000 people, every day. Most keep to Interstate 80, but as many as 6,400 — more than five times as many as before the warehouse boom — use local roads and state highways.</p><p>They pummel roads, belch fumes and batter the pavement, contributing to road damage that requires <a class="Link" href="https://8cmbykf0.r.us-east-1.awstrack.me/L0/https:%2F%2Fpublic.powerdms.com%2FIDOT%2Fdocuments%2F3173620/1/0100019e17f7fc19-52c5b68c-222b-4ab2-968a-9b44766be9f2-000000/oINe9KislV3zsNzAMBDkLDlbzds=473" target="_blank" ><u>millions of dollars</u></a> of repairs <a class="Link" href="https://8cmbykf0.r.us-east-1.awstrack.me/L0/https:%2F%2Fidot.illinois.gov%2Fabout-idot%2Fstay-connected%2Fidot-blog%2Fnew--41-billion-multi-year-improvement-program-is-largest-in-sta.html/1/0100019e17f7fc19-52c5b68c-222b-4ab2-968a-9b44766be9f2-000000/42vz53c9tZqG_jZa3Zx00ZTn-AY=473" target="_blank" ><u>paid</u></a> for by local and state governments, according to budget and grant documents.</p><p>And crashes have become more common, according to a New York Times analysis that used satellite imagery, government documents and interviews with people who live in the areas, law enforcement officers and traffic safety experts to identify some of the largest clusters of warehouses in the Chicago area. Then, using state data from January 2014 through December 2024, reporters counted the number of crashes involving trucks that occurred on the surrounding roads.</p><div class="Enhancement" Their combined square footage eclipsed that of warehouse space in the Los Angeles metropolitan area — home to the nation’s two largest shipping ports — by 13%.</p><p>Of the nation’s 25 largest metro areas, Chicago had the most warehouse square footage per person, Kerr found.</p><p>According to 2024 data, the latest available from the Illinois Department of Employment Security, warehousing and transportation was the largest sector in Will County, employing <a class="Link" href="https://8cmbykf0.r.us-east-1.awstrack.me/L0/https:%2F%2Fides.illinois.gov%2Fcontent%2Fdam%2Fsoi%2Fen%2Fweb%2Fides%2Flabor_market_information%2Fwhere_workers_work%2F2024.pdf/1/0100019e17f7fc19-52c5b68c-222b-4ab2-968a-9b44766be9f2-000000/5pbN0nvKxm_P6a0rMTWvTIUz1l4=473" target="_blank" ><u>nearly 37,000 people</u></a>. Amazon is Will County’s largest employer.</p><p>“I think people have to look at this as an economic advantage,” said Mark Denzler, president and chief executive officer of the Illinois Manufacturers’ Association.</p><p>But, for years, people living in the area have complained of miserable conditions. Some communities have taken steps to ban or limit semi-trucks on local roads, putting up signs and ticketing and fining truckers.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jamie Kelter Davis / The New York Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Some residents and local governments have taken steps to stop more development or try to reduce traffic near residential areas, with mixed results.</p><p>After Delilah LeGrett moved, in part because trucks would rumble past her front door, she found out that NorthPoint, a Kansas City-based developer, wanted to move in, too. Her house is along the edge of a proposed logistics complex in Will County that, if completed, would be five<b> </b>times the size of Midway Airport.</p><p>The complex has faced lawsuits filed by, among others, LeGrett and her neighbors, locking up development and construction. But a settlement last year ironed out truck-route access, and the pending outcome of suits this year means the facility could soon break ground.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Delilah Legrette, a lifelong resident of Manhattan, started the group Just Say No to NorthPoint in 2017 and helped lead opposition to the proposed construction of a large intermodal facility. “We bought out here because, you know, it’s a great place to live,” she says. “We love the neighborhood, all of those things. But also, you know what? They’re not going to stick behind us a warehouse because we are nowhere near anywhere that would have a warehouse. And then NorthPoint comes along and says, nope, we’re going to put a million square feet directly behind your home.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jamie Kelter Davis / The New York Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>NorthPoint representatives wouldn’t comment.</p><p>According to Will County Executive Jennifer Bertino-Tarrant, the county government’s top official, the county is spending more than ever to alleviate traffic, make streets safer and reduce air pollution.</p><p>Manhattan, where Chance Hunnicutt died, has increased its number of officers on truck enforcement patrol over the past five years. from three to eight. </p><p>Following Chance’s death, officials put stop signs at the intersection of U.S. Route 52 and North Street, where he was hit. But the signs are a temporary measure until a permanent solution is determined.</p><p>Ryan Gulli, Manhattan’s police chief, said the accident is under investigation. No charges have been filed.</p><p>Chance loved the Grateful Dead, Purdue basketball and reptiles. He and his twin brother wanted to open pet shop when they grew up: Ryder would run the business, and Chance, who dreamed of becoming a veterinarian, would take care of the animals.</p><p>“I just keep waiting for him to come out of his room,” Hunnicutt said. “There’s a big part of me that just can’t swallow the fact that he’s gone.”</p><p>About two weeks before Hunnicutt lost his son, another son lost his father when a semi turned onto Route 53. The truck collided with a Dodge Dart, killing the Dodge’s driver, 40-year-old Adam Sigler.</p><p>His 2-year-old son, who was strapped in the back seat, survived.</p><p><i>Cam Rodriguez, a Chicago Public Media data reporter who grew up in Bolingbrook, reported this story as part of The New York Times’s</i><a class="Link" href="https://www.nytco.com/careers/early-career-opportunities/local-investigations-fellowship/" target="_blank" ><i> <u>Local Investigations Fellowship</u></i></a><i>. This article was reported in partnership with Big Local News at Stanford University.</i></p><p><i>Contributing: Justin Mayo, Daniel Wood, Cheryl Phillips</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c30000" name="module-c30000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>ABOUT THE ANALYSIS</h3><br>The New York Times used satellite images, property records, government reports and other documents to identify 34 clusters of warehouse development in the Chicago area. Though not a comprehensive list, it includes the highest-profile complexes in the region.<br><br>Reporters drew a box around each group of warehouses, capturing the facilities and nearby major roads, intersections and interstate ramps. The boxes varied in size. Then, they counted accidents within those boundaries using a database obtained from the Illinois Department of Transportation, which included crashes from 2014 to 2024.<br><br>Reporters cross-referenced the department’s records with data from the Motor Carrier Management Information System to ensure that only accidents involving commercial trucks were included in the analysis.<br><br>The change in daily truck traffic was calculated using average daily traffic counts from the most recent year of available data in the 2002 and 2025 data releases, published by IDOT. This analysis used IDOT’s heavy commercial vehicle category, which includes single- and multi-unit trucks that have six or more tires.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Woman injured in Little Village mass shooting last month dies
entries.summary: <p>A woman who was injured in a mass shooting in Little Village last month died Monday. </p><p>The woman, 47, was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/22/little-village-shooting-one-dead-three-injured-26th-street" target="_blank" >among four people shot April 22</a> in the 3400 block of West 26th Street, Chicago police said. </p><p>She was pronounced dead at 5:45 p.m. Monday, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office. An autopsy is scheduled.</p><p>A man who was struck multiple times in the body died shortly after the shooting at Mt. Sinai Hospital. </p><p>Area 4 detectives were investigating. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Woman critically injured in Humboldt Park hit-and-run
entries.summary: <p>Police are looking for a maroon-colored vehicle that left the scene after hitting a 45-year-old pedestrian, critically hurting her Monday night in the Humboldt Park neighborhood.</p><p>She was walking north in the 3100 block of West Franklin Boulevard just before 8 p.m. when she was struck by a a maroon-colored vehicle going east, Chicago police said. </p><p>She was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital with head injuries and was listed in critical condition, police said. </p><p>The Major Accidents Investigations Unit was looking into the incident. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Man seriously wounded in shootout with police in South Chicago
entries.summary: <p>A shootout between a 26-year-old gunman and two Chicago police officers left the gunman seriously hurt Monday night in the South Chicago neighborhood. </p><p>Around 10:35 p.m., officers responded to a person with a gun call in the 8200 block of S. South Shore Drive and stopped a man matching a description in the 3100 block of East 83rd Street, police said. </p><p>Officers approached the man, attempted to de-escalate, and provided direction for him to keep his hands visible but an exchange of gunfire erupted between the man and two officers who fired their weapons, police said. </p><p>The man was shot in the body and was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center where he was in serious condition, authorities said. </p><p>Both officers were taken to area hospitals for observation, police said. </p><p>A gun was was recovered on the scene.</p><p>The Civilian Office of Police Accountability was investigating the shooting. The officers involved will be placed on routine administrative duties for at least 30 days. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Stop burdening working families; tax wealth and corporate profits fairly
entries.summary: <p>Washington is cutting funding. Costs are rising. Critical services are on the line. And Springfield is running out of time to choose a side.</p><p>The Trump administration's cuts to Medicaid, food assistance and public K-12 and higher education will blow a hole in our state budget. For example, Illinois could lose as much as <a class="Link" href="https://capitolnewsillinois.com/news/human-service-advocates-are-worried-after-pritzkers-budget-proposal/" target="_blank" >$51 billion</a> in federal Medicaid funding over the next 10 years — fallout from the Republican budget signed by President Donald Trump.</p><p>These are the programs that keep families fed, children in school and seniors out of poverty. When Washington walks away from those commitments, the burden doesn't disappear. It gets pushed onto states, local governments and families. Illinois has already slashed spending on core services by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/05/01/progressives-illinois-social-services-funding-bears-megaproject-economy-taxes-rich-miller" >13% since 2000</a>. We have been doing more with less for a generation.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d60000" name="module-d60000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Without sustainable new state revenue, the required cuts will be real, and they will be brutal: food assistance gone, health care access limited, economic opportunity narrowed and basic needs unmet for the people who can least afford it. At the same time, rising costs on everything from groceries to gas to rent are already squeezing Illinois families.</p><p>Illinois has one of the most unfair tax systems in the country. We rank <a class="Link" href="Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy" target="_blank" >eighth most-regressive</a> among all states, according to the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy. It also found that low-income households pay more than double the share of their income in state and local taxes compared to the wealthiest 1%. </p><p>Middle-class families’ burden keeps growing while large corporations exploit loopholes to shrink their bills. And when the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/illinois-house/2026/04/23/illinois-house-millionaires-tax-2028-state-voting-rights-amendment" >Millionaire’s Tax Amendment</a> failed to advance in Springfield last month, one of the clearest paths to fixing that imbalance was deferred until at least 2028.</p><h3>6 tax proposals </h3><h3></h3><p>The path forward isn't closed. More than 40 lawmakers in the Affordability and Tax Justice Coalition have identified six proposals that would generate the revenue Illinois needs without asking working people to pay more.</p><p><b>Tax Big Tech's data profits.</b> Technology corporations are harvesting your personal data and selling it to advertisers for billions. <a class="Link" href="https://ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=4894&GAID=18&DocTypeID=HB&LegId=166185&SessionID=114" target="_blank" >Proposed</a> <a class="Link" href="https://ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=3353&GAID=18&DocTypeID=SB&LegId=166224&SessionID=114" target="_blank" >bills</a> would impose a 10% tax on digital advertising revenue for any corporation making more than $150 million from those ads. This is a tax on the tech giants who have profited enormously from our data while contributing far too little in return.</p><p><b>Cut loose from Trump's corporate tax giveaways. </b>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.americanprogress.org/article/7-ways-the-big-beautiful-bill-cuts-taxes-for-the-rich/" target="_blank" >federal Republican budget</a> (H.R. 1, also known as the "One Big Beautiful Bill Act") handed corporations new tax loopholes, and because Illinois automatically follows federal tax law, those loopholes became Illinois loopholes too. Bills in the Illinois <a class="Link" href="https://ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=5125&GAID=18&DocTypeID=HB&LegId=166713&SessionID=114" target="_blank" >House</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=3796&GAID=18&DocTypeID=SB&LegId=167119&SessionID=114" target="_blank" >Senate</a> would reclaim revenue that corporations are now pocketing.</p><p><b>Make corporations pay what the law already allows.</b> Illinois' base corporate income tax rate is <a class="Link" href="https://tax.illinois.gov/research/taxrates/income.html" target="_blank" >7%</a>. The <a class="Link" href="https://lrb.ilga.gov/Commission/lrb/con9.htm" target="_blank" >state Constitution</a> allows it to go up to 7.92%, with no constitutional amendment needed. Bringing the state rate to its constitutional ceiling is the bare minimum.</p><p><b>Tax billionaire wealth, not just billionaire wages. </b>The wealthiest Illinoisans have found a way to avoid income taxes: Don't take income. Instead, they accumulate wealth through appreciating assets like stocks, real estate and investments that are never taxed until sold.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=5215&GAID=18&DocTypeID=HB&LegId=166888&SessionID=114" target="_blank" >Two</a> <a class="Link" href="https://ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=3376&GAID=18&DocTypeID=SB&LegId=166257&SessionID=114" target="_blank" >bills</a> would enact a tax on unrealized capital gains, ensuring that billionaires are held to the same income tax expectations as teachers, nurses and construction workers.</p><p><b>Stop the offshore shell game. </b>Large corporations can shuffle profits to subsidiaries in tax havens, reducing what they owe to Illinois taxpayers. <a class="Link" href="https://ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=5318&GAID=18&DocTypeID=HB&LegId=167073&SessionID=114" target="_blank" >Proposed</a> <a class="Link" href="https://ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=3486&GAID=18&DocTypeID=SB&LegId=166487&SessionID=114" target="_blank" >legislation </a>would enact worldwide combined reporting, closing that escape hatch and requiring corporations to account for their global profits honestly.</p><p><b>Close luxury loopholes for millionaires. </b>Illinoisans who earn over $1 million a year pay the flat income tax on just 25.8% of their income, because high earners use credits, deductions and exemptions to shrink their taxable income to a fraction of what they actually earn. </p><p>Limiting those loopholes for filers above $1 million would bring a measure of fairness to a system that has long been tilted against ordinary taxpayers.</p><h3>Social services under pressure</h3><p>Taken together, these six proposals represent a serious, structural shift toward a tax system that works for everyone, not just those at the top.</p><p>We are not asking working families to pay more. We support finding efficiencies and eliminating waste wherever it exists. </p><p>The idea that Illinois can cut its way out of this crisis — that gutting services for families already under pressure is somehow the responsible choice — is a fiction. The math doesn't support it, and it would be deeply irresponsible to force working families to bear the cost of a budget crisis created in large part by the wealthy and large corporations failing to pay their fair share.</p><p>The state lawmakers of the Affordability and Tax Justice Coalition are ready to act. We are asking our colleagues in Springfield to join us — and we are asking Illinois residents to demand it.</p><p>Washington has made its choice. Now we have to make ours in Springfield.</p><p><i>State Rep. Carol Ammons, D-Urbana, state Sen. Graciela Guzmán, D-Chicago, and state Sen. Dave Koehler, D-Peoria, are members of the Affordability and Tax Justice Coalition.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c30000" name="module-c30000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Willie Horton-style tactics continue to poison politics
entries.summary: <p>In politics, fear has a color.</p><p>For most of American history, that color has been Black.</p><p>No ad has taught that lesson more brutally than the Willie Horton ad of 1988. It showed the face of a Black man convicted of murder. It blamed Michael Dukakis for a furlough program. It told voters mercy was dangerous.</p><p>After that, clemency withered. Democrats especially learned to treat grace as a trap. To this day, too many Democratic politicians fear using their clemency powers. Even when their cowardice means people receive punishment they do not deserve.</p><p>Republican governors and presidents have often been more sweeping. Our nation’s current president has used the pardon power boldly and repeatedly. He has never seemed afraid of the power itself. Too many Democrats still are.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-0f0000" name="module-0f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>This spring marks 10 years since the Bernie Sanders campaign made a very different kind of ad. Nearly three decades after Willie Horton, I asked the campaign to do the opposite. Put a Black man convicted of murder in a presidential ad. Not to destroy the campaign. To strengthen it.</p><p>His name was Chris Wilson.</p><p>Chris grew up in Baltimore. He saw violence young. At 17, he took a man’s life. He went to prison.</p><p>There is no hiding from that truth. There should not be.</p><p>But Chris did what we say we want people to do. He took responsibility. He educated himself. He built a master plan for his life. He came home determined to work, mentor, and help others escape the traps that nearly swallowed him.</p><p>At the time, Chris was painting my house. When the campaign came to film the ad, Chris helped find the location.</p><p>To me, his story was not a liability. It was the point. Real public safety requires redemption. Prevention. Education. Jobs. Second chances.</p><p>The idea carried risk. Given the legacy of Willie Horton, some had concerns. That was understandable. This was not a safe testimonial. It was a direct challenge to a powerful racial taboo.</p><p>But in a nation with the highest incarceration rate on Earth, Willie Horton politics had trained campaigns to distrust voters. My experience told me voters were better than that.</p><p>Years earlier, I had been part of polling for a big-box retailer that wanted to know what would happen if customers learned it provided second-chance employment for formerly incarcerated people. Customers said they would be more likely to shop there. The company stood to gain market share, not lose it.</p><p>People were ready to believe in second chances. Politics just had to catch up.</p><p>Everyone signed off on taking the risk. The campaign made the ad. The name said it all: “Be Bold, Change the System.”</p><p>There was Chris, looking into the camera, telling the truth. No hiding. No sugarcoating. No mug shot. No monster. Just a man. A Black man. A Baltimore man. A man who had caused harm, paid a terrible price and fought to become a force for good.</p><p>It was the anti-Willie Horton ad.</p><p>The Willie Horton ad said Black men are the reason to fear mercy. The Chris Wilson ad said Black men are among the reasons to believe in redemption.</p><p>And it worked. The ad drew roughly a million clicks in the first 24 hours. It sent Bernie’s support up fast in Illinois. It was used powerfully in Michigan and Missouri. It moved people because it trusted them.</p><p>Chris later received a book contract. "The Master Plan" told how he refused to let prison be the end of his life. That work became the basis for an education program that has trained more than 100,000 incarcerated people.</p><p>Today, Chris is a celebrated artist whose paintings sell for tens of thousands of dollars.</p><p>That is what Willie Horton politics never wants America to see. It wants to freeze a Black man forever at the worst moment of his life. Chris Wilson proves something else. Redemption does not erase accountability. It fulfills it.</p><p>Ten years later, the lesson is urgent. Willie Horton politics is still with us. It has changed targets. Today, the scary Black man in the old ad has too often become the scary brown immigrant in the new one. Campaigns still take one terrible crime, attach it to a whole people, and tell voters mercy, due process,and fairness will get them killed.</p><p>The faces change. The formula does not.</p><p>The Chris Wilson ad, and the life he has led since, prove the best way to combat racist, authoritarian propaganda is with the bold and transformative truth.</p><p>Bold enough to believe accountability and redemption can live in the same sentence. Bold enough to trust voters with the full humanity of a Black man who changed his life. Bold enough to bury the politics Willie Horton made famous — and build a politics worthy of the people of every color we too often leave behind.</p><p>In America, the color of trust is the color of the blood in all our hearts — red and blue, flowing together as one.</p><p><i>Ben Jealous is a professor of practice at the University of Pennsylvania and former president and CEO of the NAACP.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-430000" name="module-430000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Fiance's friend has shown himself to be a cheater
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I'm engaged to a wonderful man. We are incredibly happy, and I cannot wait for our life together to begin. There's just one problem — his best friend, "Joey." Joey is wonderful to my fiance and a nice person overall, but he's a serial cheater.</p><p>In the five years I've known him, Joey has dated and cheated on multiple women, some of whom I befriended before recognizing the pattern. It's always the same — Joey meets a woman, quickly gets into something deep and monogamous, and then, after six months, he starts sleeping with other people.</p><p>Six weeks into meeting his most recent woman, they got married in a courthouse wedding. I'm having trouble bringing myself to meet his bride. I know the pattern. I know Joey will cheat after their honeymoon period ends. She certainly won't be around very long.</p><p>I feel myself getting angry, and I'm nervous about actually being in a room with them. His friends have accepted what he's like and are used to the revolving door. I want to be respectful to my fiance and meet his best friend's new wife, and I realize this is something I am going to have to deal with our entire lives, if they remain friends.</p><p>As a feminist, however, I am having trouble watching him do this to woman after woman, and I'm still expected to meet and befriend each one. How can I deal with this? — <i>WRITING ON THE WALL IN ILLINOIS</i></p><p><b>DEAR W.O.T.W.:</b> Deal with this by being a lady, meeting the new "Mrs. Joey," and being as kind to her as you would want her to be if the situation were reversed. And while you're at it, hold a good thought. This is the first woman to get Joey to the altar, and while the odds may not be great, the union might just work out. Stranger things have happened.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My parents divorced nearly 50 years ago, when I was 11. Both of my parents remarried, though Dad is now a widower. A few years ago, Dad decided he couldn't keep the secret anymore and shared it with another of my siblings and me. Our mom cheated on Dad for years, and our youngest sib, "Dana," has a different father. At first, I was angry at her (though not surprised), but I'm calmer now.</p><p>In today's age of DNA testing, I imagine Dana might find out. Wouldn't it be better if Dana knew while our parents (who are in their 80s) are alive and could explain? Dana's biological father is deceased, and Dad has been a wonderful father to all of us kids.</p><p>I don't want to cause any pain, yet I'm having a hard time keeping this to myself. My spouse suggests I talk with Mom, gently let her know that I'm aware of the situation, and ask if Dana already knows. I'm torn. — <i>HEAVY SECRET</i></p><p><b>DEAR SECRET:</b> Your spouse's instinct is correct. You need to talk about this, so it makes sense to speak to someone who already knows the secret. Clearing the air with your mom will make you feel better, and it may give her the strength to come clean with Dana if that's what she thinks is best.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>Good advice for everyone — teens to seniors — is in "The Anger in All of Us and How to Deal With It." To order, send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds) to: Dear Abby, Anger Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: How to make Kouklas’ whipped feta
entries.summary: <p>At Kouklas Greek Eatery, this whipped feta is one of those dishes that seems simple but leaves a lasting impression. Created by chefs Jimmy Bannos Jr. and Kevin Stack, it’s rich, tangy and incredibly smooth — something guests immediately want to recreate at home after their first bite. In Greek cooking, feta is often served in its natural form, but this version transforms it into a lighter, more spreadable dish while still holding onto its bold, briny character.</p><p>We balance high-quality feta cheese with creamy Greek yogurt and cream cheese to create a texture that’s both airy and indulgent. It’s versatile enough to serve as a dip, a spread or even as a base under grilled meats.</p><p>Whether you keep it classic with olive oil and cucumbers or add heat with charred peppers, this is a dish that brings people to the table and keeps them coming back.</p><h3>Whipped Feta</h3><p><b>Ingredients</b><br>1 2/3 cup feta cheese (preferably Valbresa or another soft feta)<br>1 2/3 cup cream cheese (such as Philadelphia), room temperature<br>3/4 cup Greek yogurt (full-fat)</p><p><b>Directions</b></p><p>Add the cream cheese to a food processor and blend until completely smooth.</p><p>Add the Greek yogurt and feta.</p><p>Blend until fully combined and silky, scraping down the sides as needed.</p><p>To serve, transfer to a shallow bowl. Top with diced cucumbers and finish with a drizzle of high-quality Greek extra virgin olive oil.</p><p>Serve with warm bread or alongside fresh vegetables like sliced cucumbers.</p><p><b>Variations</b></p><p><b>Spicy Whipped Feta</b></p><p>Char a Fresno chile pepper until blistered. Remove the skin and blend it in with the feta and cream cheese. For added color and sweetness, blend in Florina peppers or any roasted red peppers.</p><p>Finish with diced roasted red peppers and a drizzle of olive oil.</p><p><b>Chef’s Note</b></p><p>This spread isn’t just for dipping — try spreading it across the bottom of a plate and placing hot grilled meat skewers directly on top. The whipped feta melts slightly underneath, creating a rich, flavorful base.</p>
entries.author: Jimmy Bannos Jr. and Kevin Stack | Kouklas

entries.title: A Chicago museum is reissuing John Wayne Gacy's book
entries.summary: <p>Ryan Manon has been collecting John Wayne Gacy “murderabilia” for decades. He has spent hundreds of thousands of dollars, and much of his 44 years, amassing more than 300 original paintings, letters, logbooks and other ephemera connected to Gacy, who raped and murdered 33 young men and boys before burying them in a subterranean crawl space on the Northwest Side.</p><p>Manon’s holdings include a lengthy, unpublished death row manuscript Gacy wrote going back to his earliest memories. Manon estimates his collection at 30,000 items, which includes the killer’s brain in a jar in the Chicago suburbs.</p><p>“I am definitely sort of the foremost authority on Gacy,” said Manon from his Savannah, Ga. museum-gallery. “Literally I own everything and I know everything.”</p><p>It’s an obsession, he says, and it may yet break him.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Inside the museums, visitors can find a cornucopia of other items that are weird, strange, awful, fascinating and revolting.</p><p>Copies of the book will be available for sale for $40 at 1829 N. Milwaukee Avenue, and online at their website, <a class="Link" href="http://graveface.com" target="_blank" ><u>GravefaceMuseum.com</u></a>.</p><p>The 352-page book, with a press run of 500 copies, is the latest unboxed cultural artifact in the seemingly never-ending fascination with the prolific serial killer. The cold case counts five unidentified victims, and is still open under the jurisdiction of Cook County Sheriff Thomas Dart. The book’s publication date of Sunday is also notable: 32 years to the day after the 52-year-old Gacy was executed following his murder conviction in 1980. The book was originally titled “The 34th Victim.”</p><p>“The case just never ends,” one of Gacy’s death row attorneys, Karen Conti, said in 2021. “There will always be a fascination with John Wayne Gacy. Always.”</p><p>Conti was prophetic. Peacock last fall released a dramatized mini-series <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2025/10/15/john-wayne-gacy-devil-in-disguise-michael-chernus" target="_blank" ><u>“Devil in Disguise”</u></a>, starring Michael Chernus. It follows the network’s excellent five-part documentary of the same name from 2021, which is largely the work of two Chicagoans, journalist Alison True and producer Tracy Ullman.</p><div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The reprint of “A Question of Doubt” will include an introduction by Karen Gacy (right), John Wayne Gacy’s sister, who died in 2024. Here, she’s pictured before her death with Chloe Manon (left) and Ryan Manon (center).</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Ryan Manon</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The Graveface franchise hopes the book will be “a piece of the puzzle” to what they say are unanswered questions. Having wrangled the book back to life after five years of work, the two sound almost apologetic. Chloe Manon calls the book “annoying”; Ryan Manon calls it full of the convicted killer’s “ramblings.”</p><p>But Ryan believed the book rerelease is important so that the legions of Gacy aficionados, amateur sleuths and voyeurs wouldn’t have to shell out more than $2,000 for one of the 500 original copies, he says.</p><p>“I’ve never viewed true crime as a way to make money,” he said.</p><p>Admittedly, for the few who’ve been able to get their hands on a copy of the original, there’s not much new, except for an introduction by Karen Gacy, who remained close with a brother she nonetheless believed was guilty of murder (she died in 2024). Besides selling and renting a large collection of hard to find underground and cult horror films and vinyl, the museum has several small rooms with displays on: circus sideshows, cults, the occult, taxidermy, psychiatric wards and other serial killers.</p><p>The Gacy room is kitted out as his death row jail cell, with bars and a cot. Gacy paintings, photos and letters cover the walls, while a small monitor silently plays a death row interview. A page from Gacy’s prison logbook shows a jam-packed schedule of phone calls, letter-writing and personal meetings with people like criminology instructor James Sparks.</p><p>Gacy ran a virtual mail-order business out of his prison cell and spent hours each day churning out new paintings on commission. He painted an estimated 2,400 canvases during his life and even had a 1-900 pay-per-call phone number. Watching all this money come in, the state of Illinois tried to recoup some of the costs of his prison stay, though it eventually gave up.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-de0000" name="image-de0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d1aa953/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F14%2F1e7ae8fa4871993407dc03b1e209%2Fgacybook-260510-18.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/eec7e8c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F14%2F1e7ae8fa4871993407dc03b1e209%2Fgacybook-260510-18.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6225bf2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F14%2F1e7ae8fa4871993407dc03b1e209%2Fgacybook-260510-18.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Paintings, letters, and notes from the Question of Doubt John Wayne Gacy exhibit at Graveface Museum Chicago at 1829 N. Milwaukee Ave. in Wicker Park, Thursday, May 7, 2026." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6225bf2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F14%2F1e7ae8fa4871993407dc03b1e209%2Fgacybook-260510-18.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ad0f7c6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F14%2F1e7ae8fa4871993407dc03b1e209%2Fgacybook-260510-18.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6225bf2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F14%2F1e7ae8fa4871993407dc03b1e209%2Fgacybook-260510-18.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Gacy ran a virtual mail-order business out of his prison cell and spent hours each day churning out new paintings on commission.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>But that long residence produced a lot of collectible materials, which appeals to Ryan Manon’s "classic hoarder” instincts. Ryan, whose obsession with the serial killer began as a Chicago teenager, bought his first Gacy painting, a “skull clown” for $500, and later bought the estate of a Gacy collector for $700, which included a cache of audio cassettes.</p><p>Watching the market accelerate for Gacy paintings, including bootlegs, Ryan has added to his menu of services authentication of originals using the prison logbook he got from Karen Gacy.</p><p>Interest in Gacy does not seem to wane over the years. Cook County Sheriff Dart reopened the case in 2011 and using new DNA technology was able to identify three of the eight remaining unidentified victims, the most recent in 2021.</p><p>For his part, Manon believes questions still remain, claiming that there are over 100 Gacy victims, including in other states, and at least seven accomplices who have not been held to account, as well as a much larger pedophile ring that authorities failed to fully investigate.</p><p>Cook County Sheriff’s Officer Commander Jason Moran, a 28-year veteran who came up with the idea of reopening the cold case and has been directing the work ever since, said he has investigated those claims and never found sufficient evidence of other Gacy victims, accomplices or connections to a pedophile ring. The DNA work continues to unfold slowly but Morgan says he hopes to identify some or all of the remaining Gacy victims before he retires in a few years.</p>
